Long before the Universal Declaration of Human Rights took shape, the UN General Assembly passed Resolution 43 on 11 December 1946. The Economic and Social Council had set up a Commission on Human Rights that year. Its charge was to draft plans for an international bill of rights. A draft Declaration on Fundamental Human Rights and Freedoms was already in hand.

The Assembly sends that draft to the council, for the commission to use as it drafts the bill. It also voices the hope that the question will come back to the Assembly in time for its second regular session. The path from this referral led, two years later, to the famous 1948 declaration.

The sole sure defense, it argues, is their total end, with a pledge they will never be made again.

The pledges of the nuclear states are spelled out: the firm vow of 2000 to wipe out their arsenals in full. Deep concern at the toll of any use of such arms runs through the vote. The Conference on Disarmament is pressed to open talks on a phased plan, with a set frame of time.

Days after the Republic of the Congo gained independence, its government asked the United Nations for military help, and Belgium still had troops on Congolese soil. Resolution 143, adopted on 14 July 1960, was the Security Council's first answer to the Congo Crisis. The vote was eight to none, with three abstentions.

The Council calls on Belgium to withdraw its troops from the Congo. It authorizes the Secretary-General, in consultation with the Congolese government, to provide military assistance until Congo's own security forces can fully do their job, with UN technical help. He must report back to the Council. The decision launched one of the UN's largest early peacekeeping efforts.

Olivier Neyrolles, Rogelio Hernández-Pando, France Pietri-Rouxel, and co-authors asked a pointed question in 2006: does tuberculosis hide in fat? Mycobacterium tuberculosis can sleep inside the body for years before waking to cause disease. Its hiding places were thought to be mainly in the lungs and immune cells.

The team tested adipose tissue, body fat, as a place of persistence. Fat is plentiful, long-lived, and laced with immune cells, which makes it a plausible bunker. If the germ truly shelters there, treatment must reach it there too, and relapse after cure becomes easier to explain. The question opened a line of research into fat as an overlooked reservoir in chronic infection.

Secretary of State Cordell Hull wrote to President Roosevelt on 21 November 1943 about sparing Rome. His letter carries a draft message to the Pope, ready for Roosevelt's signature, on recognizing Rome as an open city.

Hull argues that, for reasons beyond the military ones, America should make a sincere effort to save Rome from the ruin of modern war. If no deal is reached, she should leave the blame for refusal with the Germans. The draft letter tells the Pope that Washington accepts the Italian government's August declaration and its conditions, if Germany grants the same status. One reservation is spelled out: Allied forces keep full transit rights through Rome by rail and road.

The final text of the Cairo communiqué, dated 26 November 1943, is the agreed statement of the first Cairo Conference. Harry Hopkins handed the text to Ambassador Kirk that afternoon, and the White House released it to the press on 1 December, after the Tehran meeting ended.

The statement says the military missions have agreed on future operations against Japan, and that the three allies will bring unrelenting pressure by sea, land, and air. The three powers covet no gain and no territory. Japan will be stripped of all Pacific islands seized since 1914. The territories stolen from China, including Manchuria, Formosa, and the Pescadores, will be restored. Japan will be expelled from every land taken by violence and greed. Korea, in due course, will become free and independent.

By December 5, 1943, the Second Cairo Conference was in full swing, and the Combined Chiefs of Staff met again that day. Their minutes, printed in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume, come from the joint body that matched American and British plans into one war effort. Turkey's possible entry into the war hung over the whole conference.

The record follows the chiefs through the day's military business, with positions stated, differences worked through, and decisions noted for the two heads of government. Read beside the Tehran documents, it shows the alliance moving from promises to planning. Few sources show wartime teamwork at this level so plainly.

President Roosevelt addressed this message on January 10, 1944 to Patrick J. Hurley, his personal representative, then temporarily in Iran. Hurley, a former secretary of war, roamed the Middle East on the President's personal business. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

The Acting Secretary of State wrote to the Secretary of State on 22 July 1945. The Washington end of the circuit answered the summit end on a near daily rhythm. Grew's messages carried the home office's news and needs to Byrnes in Germany.

By the second week, the circuit was a settled habit. Files moved, questions rose, and answers came back within a day or two. This cable is one turn of that habit. Small in itself, it belongs to a rare system. That system let one department sit in two places at once, in the most crowded fortnight of its year.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1343:
A text handed in by the Soviet delegation on 29 July 1945 forms document 1343 of the Potsdam volume. It came in the last days of the conference, when drafting of the final papers was at its most intense. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Late texts at a summit often carry the hardest bargaining, since each side knows the clock is running out. What a delegation chose to put in writing at that stage shows what it valued most. Set beside the closing protocol, this Soviet text helps readers judge the talks. It shows how much of the Soviet program survived, and how much was traded away.
frus-1945-50-intel-d43:
Ladd, an assistant director of the FBI, wrote to Hoover on 5 November 1945. Ladd ran much of the bureau's intelligence and security work and stood high in Hoover's trust. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

Assistant directors' memoranda gave Hoover the bureau's own picture of events, filtered by men who knew his mind. Ladd's paper belongs to the FBI's watch on the central intelligence question, which touched the bureau's foreign operations directly. Readers building the FBI thread should set Ladd beside Tamm: two senior aides serving one director. Their stream of paper kept the bureau's position sharp through the long contest of 1945 and 1946.
frus-1945-50-intel-d143:
A memorandum dated 14 February 1946 links two senior offices. The sender was the Director of Central Intelligence (Souers). The reader was the Secretary of State’s Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (McCormack). The State Department prints it as document 143 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The postwar system was still new: the National Intelligence Authority gave the orders, and the Central Intelligence Group carried them out.

Such notes moved business along: they told a busy reader what had happened, what it meant, and what should come next. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d243:
A memorandum by the Army Member of the State–Army–Navy–Air Force Coordinating Committee (Pixtou) bears the date 15 October 1947. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 243 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. The CIA was only weeks old, having replaced the Central Intelligence Group in September 1947 under the National Security Act.

Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings. One put the question and the facts in front of the reader at once. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d343:
A memorandum dated 17 March 1948 links two senior offices. The sender was the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers). The reader was Allen W. Dulles, Mathias F. Correa, and William H. Jackson. The State Department prints it as document 343 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Across Washington, the new security bodies were moving from setup work to the real business of the Cold War.

Such notes moved business along: they told a busy reader what had happened, what it meant, and what should come next. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1861-d43:
On 27 April 1861, William H. Seward sent orders to Charles Francis Adams, his new envoy to Britain. The letter is document 43 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Adams was then crossing to take up the London post. Seward's April orders framed the line he should take with the British government. Britain had yet to state its stance on the war, and each word from Washington would shape Adams's first talks. Adams reached London in mid May and found a government still making up its mind. Mind and map were both still open when Adams stepped ashore in May.
frus-1861-d143:
Writing on 17 August 1861, William H. Seward reset his orders to William Dayton for a long war. The letter is document 143 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward's mid August letters have a plainer, graver tone than those of June. The short war was gone, and the orders fit the new facts. This note to Paris shows policy reset for endurance: fewer boasts, firmer law, longer watch. The reset he describes governed the Paris file through the rest of 1861. Endurance as policy asked envoys to be dull on cue, and Dayton obliged. Endurance, as policy, asked for dull strength.
frus-1861-d243:
James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands was the reader in mind when William H. Seward wrote on 8 July 1861. It stands as Document 243 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. It was written in the first summer of the Civil War, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d43:
Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London was the reader in mind when William H. Seward wrote on 3 April 1862. It stands as Document 43 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. The date falls in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d143:
Orders from Washington reached Charles Francis Adams in a State Department letter dated 15 September 1862. It stands as Document 143 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. The date falls in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d243:
William Stuart wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 12 October 1862, and the letter closes the Stuart run as Document 243 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Stuart had led the British legation through the summer and early fall.

By mid-October, the British cabinet was moving toward a decision against stepping into the war, though Stuart could not know its final shape. His letters across these months form a distinct chapter in the record: an understudy handling a great post in a crisis. This last letter ends that chapter on the eve of the decision. Both offices kept up the formal courtesies even when their governments were near quarreling.
frus-1862-d343:
The third Seward dispatch of 4 November 1862 stands as Document 343 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Like its mates, it went from Secretary of State William H. Seward to William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris.

Within days, the British cabinet voted down the truce proposal, and the fall crisis ended. These letters were already at sea, written for a danger that was passing. The overlap is a fine lesson in 1862 statecraft. Policy had to be framed to hold in several futures, because no one could know which future had begun. France's Mexican venture shared the court's attention with the American war all year.
frus-1862-d443:
On 6 May 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Norman B. Judd, the American minister at Berlin. The instruction is Document 443 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

By May 1862 Union victories in the West and the fall of New Orleans gave Seward good news to send his ministers. Judd's post in Berlin was a friendly place to send it. Prussia had no wish to aid the Confederacy, but its court still had to be courted and kept informed. Instructions of this sort also told ministers how to answer Confederate claims abroad. The dispatch shows Washington working a friendly capital with the same care it gave to doubtful ones.
frus-1862-d543:
Roest van Limburg wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 30 August 1862, the second day of the battle of Second Bull Run. His note is Document 543 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

That a Dutch minister transacted calm formal business in Washington while a battle raged thirty miles away is itself a fact about wartime capitals. Van Limburg's errand remained the protection of Dutch interests, which the war touched through trade and shipping rather than armies. His note belongs to the late-summer Dutch file, where the tone stayed correct even as the military news darkened. Seward's department answered such notes as they came, and the printed sequence preserves that discipline.
frus-1862-d643:
Townsend Harris sent this dispatch from Japan to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 23 November 1861. It is Document 643 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, accompanying the annual message.

Harris wrote in late November, as the Trent affair was breaking in the Atlantic world he could not hear of for months. In Edo his business remained the treaty relationship and the condition of the mission he had founded. He was by then a sick man nearing the end of his service. His remaining letters have the quality of a founder setting his house in order. The dispatch is among the last of his printed reports in the volume, closing the first chapter of American diplomacy in Japan.
frus-1863p1-d43:
Judah P. Benjamin sent this letter to John Slidell on 28 October 1862. Benjamin was the Confederate secretary of state; Slidell was the South's envoy in Paris. The letter is document 43 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

By late October the South's drive for foreign backing was losing ground, after Antietam and the first word of the freedom edict. Benjamin's letters to Paris kept the push alive on paper. This one is a late-fall piece of that effort. Printed by the Union in its own volume, it shows the other side's hopes in its own hand, at the hour they began to fade.
frus-1863p1-d143:
On 3 April 1863, Charles Francis Adams sent a second dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 143 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, the middle piece of three sent that day.

The middle sheet of Adams's sets often held the day's weight. In April 1863 the weight was ships: Southern raiders built in Britain, and the Union's drive to stop them. This letter holds its place in that fight's record. Read with its mates, it shows the legation working all its lines at once in the war's most fraught spring abroad.
frus-1863p1-d243:
Washington's orders to London on 23 July 1863 came in this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 243 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Instructions like this one show how the Lincoln government ran a war abroad while fighting one at home. The paper trail is the diplomacy itself, order by order. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d343:
In Washington on 22 December 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 343 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Lyons was the man Seward had to persuade, warn, or answer in person in Washington. Notes to him carried the American side of each dispute between the two governments. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d443:
Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington received a letter dated 3 April 1863 from William H. Seward, the Secretary of State. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d543:
The letter printed as document 543 was written on 30 May 1863 by F. W. Seward to Lord Lyons. F. W. Seward was the Assistant Secretary of State, writing here to Britain's minister in Washington. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d643:
William H. Seward took up his pen on 23 October 1863 and wrote to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

That autumn the sharpest issue was the pair of ironclad rams built for the Confederacy at Birkenhead. Britain held them back, and this mail ran while that fight played out. British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
plos-pbio-0020243:
Anne E. Bygrave, Kirsten L. Rose, Josefina Cortes-Hernandez, and their team raised a caution about mouse research in PLOS Biology in 2004. Two common lab mouse strains, called 129 and C57BL/6, can develop signs of autoimmune disease on their own as they age. Autoimmunity means the immune system attacks the body itself.

That background noise can confuse studies of gene-targeted mice. If a normal mouse of the same strain shows the same signs, a removed gene may not be the cause. The authors urge care in picking control mice and in reading results. Their warning helps labs avoid false claims about which genes cause lupus-like disease in mice.
plos-pone-0000143:
Peter Caley, Niels G. Becker, and David J. Philp published this modeling study in PLOS ONE in 2007. It asks a pointed question for pandemic planning: once influenza erupts in one country, how long is the waiting time before it spreads to others? The authors build a model of that inter-country spread.

The answer shapes how much time health agencies have to react with travel measures, vaccines, or alerts. The authors weigh factors that shorten or lengthen the delay. Their work belongs to the planning literature that tries to turn the chaos of the last pandemic into numbers the next response can use.
plos-pone-0000243:
Margarita Gutova, Joseph Najbauer, Anna Gevorgyan, and colleagues published this lung cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Small cell lung cancer is aggressive and often resists chemotherapy. The authors identify a set of tumor cells marked by the protein uPAR that survive chemotherapy, chemoresistant cells that can regrow the cancer.

Finding the cells that outlast treatment is the key to stopping relapse. The authors show these uPAR-positive cells carry that resistant role. The marker gives drug developers a defined target: kill this subpopulation, and the tumor's comeback route may close.
plos-pone-0000343:
Olivia Carter and Patrick Cavanagh published this vision study in PLOS ONE in 2007. When two different images are shown to the two eyes, perception rivals: one image wins, then the other. The authors study onset rivalry, the contest at the very start of viewing. They show that a brief presentation isolates an early, independent phase of that perceptual competition.

Isolating the opening phase lets researchers study competition before slower influences pile on. The authors use very short displays to catch it. The result sharpens the picture of how the brain chooses what we see when the eyes disagree.
plos-pone-0000443:
Alexander Maye and colleagues searched for order in behavior with no instructions, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. When animals or people act spontaneously, their choices look random at first glance. The team analyzed spontaneous behavior for hidden structure, patterns that would show the behavior is organized rather than coin-flip random.

Finding order in spontaneity matters for how scientists interpret free behavior in experiments, from flies in a chamber to people at rest. Structured spontaneous behavior suggests the brain generates patterned activity on its own, rather than merely reacting. The paper joins a growing challenge to the idea that unprompted behavior is noise.
plos-pone-0000543:
John R. Talbott argued that the scale of sex work shapes the global AIDS pandemic, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper titled Size Matters. His analysis linked the number of prostitutes in a population to the spread of HIV/AIDS across countries. Commercial sex networks can carry the virus efficiently between high-risk and general populations.

The claim directs policy toward the structure of epidemics, not only individual behavior. Where sex work is extensive, targeted prevention may decide a country's trajectory. Such ecological analyses are debated because country-level patterns can mislead, but they force attention on drivers that clinic-based studies overlook.
plos-pone-0000643:
Timothy H.-C. Hsiau, Claudiu Diaconu, Connie A. Myers and colleagues mapped the control logic of the eye's light-sensing cells, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Photoreceptors, the retina cells that catch light, carry more genetic diseases than any other cell type. Most of the more than 120 cloned human blindness genes are highly expressed in photoreceptors.

The team studied the cis-regulatory logic, the DNA switches near genes, that runs the photoreceptor gene network. Their aim was an integrative framework, one map joining the switches to the genes they control. Such a map helps explain how photoreceptors become what they are, and why so many mutations blind.
plos-pone-0000743:
Garret Suen, Barry S. Goldman and Roy D. Welch worked on predicting where a bacterium lives from its genome alone. When they wrote in 2007, automated sequencing was so fast that analysis had become the rate-limiting step. Hundreds of prokaryotic genomes were publicly available, with new ones arriving at roughly 20 per month. Each genome is a parts list without an address.

An ecological niche describes the environment an organism occupies and the life it leads there. If gene content predicts the niche, researchers can infer lifestyle for microbes never cultured in a lab. Most microbes refuse culturing, so genome-based prediction opens the majority of bacterial life to study.
plos-pone-0000843:
Yossi Buskila, Yasmin Abu-Ghanem, Yifat Levi and colleagues reported brain support cells making a signaling gas in a mutant mouse, for PLOS ONE in 2007. It was well accepted that glial cells in the central nervous system produce nitric oxide through the enzyme NOS2 only in response to various insults. The team had recently described rapid astroglial, NOS2-dependent nitric oxide production under other conditions, challenging that rule.

In a NOS2 mutant mouse, they report enhanced astrocytic nitric oxide production and neuronal modifications in the neocortex. Astrocytes are the brain's housekeeper cells, and nitric oxide is both messenger and potential toxin. Rewriting when this gas is made changes accounts of brain inflammation and injury.
plos-pone-0000943:
Konrad Kording, Ulrik Beierholm, Wei Ji Ma and colleagues framed perception as the brain drawing conclusions about causes, in PLOS ONE in 2007. A sensation matters to an animal because of what it says about the world. Smells, sounds and sights are clues, and the brain must infer what caused them.

The authors apply that idea to multisensory perception, where several senses report at once. The brain has to decide whether two clues share one cause or come from separate events. That decision shapes whether we merge the clues or keep them apart. Their causal inference view gives a single logic for many puzzling perception results.
plos-pone-0001043:
Sherine Abboud, Pekka Karhunen, Dieter Lutjohann and colleagues linked a cholesterol gene to a major stroke type, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The gene PCSK9 helps set blood levels of LDL cholesterol, the harmful kind. Its variants were already tied to cholesterol levels and coronary heart disease severity.

The team asked whether PCSK9 also raises the risk of large vessel atherosclerosis stroke, the kind caused by clogged big arteries. A gene that links cholesterol to stroke as well as heart disease widens the case for targeting it. Drugs against PCSK9 were a live idea at the time. Genetic evidence from patients helps judge that idea.
plos-pone-0001143:
Long-term cocaine use is known to impair a person's ability to stop a behavior once started. Lorenza Colzato, Wery van den Wildenberg, and Bernhard Hommel asked whether casual users show the same problem, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Recreational users are a growing group, and findings from heavy users may not apply to them.

The study compared recreational cocaine users with non-users on tasks that require inhibiting and executing responses. Their title states the result: inhibitory control is impaired in the recreational users tested. That finding extends concern about cocaine's effects on self-control beyond chronic addiction.
plos-pone-0001243:
Insecticide-treated bed nets and sprays are mainstays of malaria control, but mosquitoes evolve resistance. João Pinto and colleagues studied knockdown resistance mutations in Anopheles gambiae, the chief African malaria mosquito, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. How often such mutations arise in wild mosquito populations is a basic question for resistance research.

The authors report multiple origins of the knockdown resistance mutations in this mosquito across the Afrotropics. Resistance did not spread from a single source; it evolved repeatedly. That changes how control programs should expect resistance to emerge and spread.
plos-pone-0001343:
Thiacetazone is an old antitubercular drug whose precise action was unclear. Anuradha Alahari and colleagues report how it works against mycobacteria, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The mycobacterial cell wall is rich in mycolic acids, complex branched fatty acids that make the wall highly hydrophobic and hard for drugs to cross.

Pathogenic mycobacteria carry mycolic acid subtypes containing cyclopropane rings. The authors show that thiacetazone inhibits the cyclopropanation of these cell wall mycolic acids. Weakening the wall's chemistry explains the drug's effect and suggests related targets for new TB drugs.
plos-pone-0001443:
Cecilia Poderoso and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how cells make steroid hormones. A signal chain known as ERK helps drive hormone based steroid making, but its exact role was vague. Both the signal and steroid making can be sparked by a cell messenger. The team traced a protein complex inside the cell power units.

They show this complex is vital for the chain to tag a key control protein. That tag is a step the cell needs to make steroids. The finding places part of the control inside the power units themselves. It refines the map that drug and hormone research relies on.
plos-pone-0001543:
Jens Schwachtje, Susan Kutschbach, and Ian Baldwin published a 2008 PLOS ONE essay on gene tests in field ecology. By tweaking single genes, labs can test what each gene does for a plant in the wild. That power could reshape plant ecology. But fears of side effects from the tweak method had held the field back.

The authors weigh those fears against the gains and set terms for sound use. Field tests with single gene changes can split gene effects from soil and weather noise. The essay urges the field to move, with care, from lab pots to real ground. It frames rules for that step.
plos-pone-0001643:
Carla Lucia Esposito and co-authors studied how two receptor proteins talk to each other in nerve tumor cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The receptors are TrkB and Ret, both tyrosine kinases, enzymes that pass growth and survival signals into the cell. How signals from several such receptors combine to set a cell's final state is a key question for drug design.

The team worked with neuroblastoma cells, a childhood nerve cancer, treated with retinoic acid, a drug that pushes these cells to mature. Their results show cross-talk: Ret treatment also brings TrkB into play, and together they drive the cells to differentiate. The full text gives the signal measurements and cell outcomes. Mapping this kind of cross-talk helps explain why some tumors resist drugs aimed at a single receptor.
plos-pone-0001743:
Hamish A. Campbell, Keiron P. P. Fraser, Charles M. Bishop, and their co-authors reported hibernation-like behavior in an Antarctic fish in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Mammals, birds, reptiles, and amphibians actively suppress metabolism ahead of winter. Fish were thought different: their metabolic rate simply falls in step with water temperature, with no active suppression.

The team's fish, studied on the ice through winter, showed an active metabolic suppression in anticipation of winter conditions. The full text gives the activity and metabolic measurements across seasons. A fish that truly hibernates rewrites a chapter of physiology. It hints at how animals first evolved winter dormancy, and it was found in one of the harshest seas on Earth.
plos-pone-0001843:
Hung Tseng, Weichin Chou, Junwen Wang, and their co-authors catalogued variants of mouse ribosomal RNA genes in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Earlier cytogenetic studies suggested the various rDNA chromosomal loci are not equally active in different cell types. Consistent with this variability, rDNA polymorphism is well documented in humans and mice.

Attempts to identify molecular rDNA variant types had lagged. The team reports that mouse ribosomal RNA genes contain multiple differentially regulated variants. The full text gives the variant sequences and their activity patterns by cell type. Ribosomes build all proteins, so regulated rRNA variants add a hidden layer to how cells tune protein production.
plos-pone-0001943:
Liora Shamgar and co-authors probed a partner protein that reins in a key channel, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The channel, Kv7.1, helps set heart rhythm and nerve firing, and faults in the Kv7 family cause heart and nerve disorders. Kv7.1 rarely works alone; a small partner, KCNE1, joins it and changes how it acts.

The team studied how KCNE1 holds back the channel's voltage sensor, the part that feels charge and works the gate. As the title states, KCNE1 constrains that sensor. Knowing the brake's grip helps explain rhythm disorders tied to this channel, and it may guide drugs that ease or tighten the hold.
plos-pone-0002043:
Wendy Stevens and co-authors checked the baseline health of African volunteers for future HIV vaccine trials, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Safe trials enroll healthy people, and lab safety values are used to screen them. Knowing the normal health profile of local volunteers is key to running such trials well, yet data from Africa were thin.

The team recorded morbidity at baseline in two thousand nine hundred ninety adult volunteers recruited to set lab reference intervals. Local reference values stop healthy Africans from being barred by norms drawn from other continents. The study lays groundwork for vaccine trials across several sites.
plos-pone-0002143:
Petteri Ilmonen, Alexander Kotrschal, and Dustin Penn asked whether fighting infection can wear down the ends of chromosomes, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Those ends, called telomeres, act as protective caps. They grow shorter as a person ages, and many scientists think that this shortening plays a part in aging itself.

A leading idea holds that inflammation is a main cause of telomere loss, since immune defense is costly for the body. Infection is one strong source of that inflammation. The authors test the idea that infections speed up telomere shortening. If true, a lifetime of fighting germs would leave a mark written into the chromosomes themselves.
plos-pone-0002243:
Anne Schulp, Mohammed Al-Wosabi, and Nancy Stevens reported the first dinosaur tracks found on the Arabian Peninsula, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The Mesozoic land animals of Arabia were almost unknown when they wrote. Despite wide rocky outcrops, only a handful of fossils had been described from the region.

Near Madar in Yemen, the team documented a track assemblage left by more than one kind of dinosaur. Footprints record living animals in motion, including herd behavior that bones alone cannot show. The find opens a blank page in the region's fossil record and suggests far more waits in Arabian rock.
plos-pone-0002343:
Inken Beck and co-authors removed an enzyme in mice to learn what it does for the immune system. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. MMP19 is a matrix metalloproteinase, an enzyme that cuts the scaffolding between cells. It affects cell proliferation, adhesion, and migration in the dish, but its real role in the body was poorly understood.

The team generated mice lacking MMP19 by disrupting its catalytic domain. They report that MMP19 is essential for normal T cell development and for T cell-driven immune responses in the skin. A scaffolding enzyme turning out to be required for immunity widens its interest for inflammation research.
plos-pone-0002443:
Mattson led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are Christine L. Mattson, Richard T. Campbell, Robert C. Bailey, among others. Its subject is risk Compensation Is Not Associated with Male Circumcision in Kisumu, Kenya. The title goes on to note a Multi-Faceted Assessment of Men Enrolled in a Randomized Controlled Trial. Three randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have confirmed that male circumcision (MC) significantly reduces acquisition of HIV-1 infection among men.

The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002543:
Rueda and other authors present their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Named on the byline are Patricia Rueda, Karl Balabanian, Bernard Lagane, among others. Its subject is the CXCL12γ Chemokine Displays Unprecedented Structural and Functional Properties that Make It a Paradigm of Chemoattractant Proteins. The CXCL12γ chemokine arises by alternative splicing from Cxcl12, an key gene during development.

This protein binds CXCR4 and displays an exceptional degree of conservation (99%) in mammals. The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002643:
Taichi E. Takasuka and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was sequence information encoded in DNA that may influence Long-Range chromatin structure correlates with human chromosome functions. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Taichi E. Takasuka, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Little is known about the possible function of the bulk of the human genome. It goes on to note a further point. We have recently shown that long-range regular oscillation in the motif non-T, A/T, G (VWG) existing at ten-nucleotide multiples influences large-scale nucleosome array formation. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002743:
Eun Jig Lee and co-authors studied a cancer-related protein called AFX in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. AFX, also known as FOXO4, belongs to the forkhead family of transcription factors, proteins that switch genes on and off. In its alpha form it acts as a tumor suppressor.
